message_source_quote: Instead of reproducing the White-Bear Steering (WBS) approach from Raman et al. 2026 — which uses a single think/don't-think contrast built from WSB's directed_modulation bank items — I built a **multi-stance ensemble** from self-authored prompt pairs
writeup_source_quote:
instead of a single think/don't-think contrast (Raman et al. 2026, who used WSB's
directed_modulation bank items), we write our own prompt pairs and pool across six
stance wordings.

differences.message_quote: Novelty: The multi-stance ensemble is a new contribution — no prior work combines stance directions across multiple wordings. It demonstrates that the active-vs-suppressive stance component is shared across phrasings and transfers to self-authored prompts independent of benchmark items.
differences.writeup_quote:
(3) A different optimal dose (scale 1.12) from the single-contrast
peak, consistent with the ensemble producing a sharper shared direction.
differences.what: the write-up lists a third novelty point — a different optimal steering dose/scale compared to the single-contrast peak — which the message's novelty summary omits

rationale: Both documents credit Raman et al. 2026 (the white-bear/WBS steering paper) explicitly by name, describe the baseline as a single think/don't-think contrast built from WSB's directed_modulation bank items, and claim the same core novelty: a multi-stance ensemble pooling six stance wordings using self-authored, benchmark-independent prompts, said to be unprecedented ('no prior work combines stance directions'). The only discrepancy is that the write-up's 'What is new' section adds a third, minor novelty point (the different optimal dose of 1.12 vs the single-contrast peak) that the message's summary leaves out, but this is a mechanism/numeric detail rather than a change in how the source or overlap is framed.
